source: Carpenter, Just and Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures: a theoretical account of Raven Progressive Matrices
finding: Founding capacity theory. FAIRAVEN and BETTERAVEN simulations solve Raven items by finding rules from a taxonomy (constant, pairwise progression, figure addition/subtraction, distribution of 3, distribution of 2). Difficulty rises with the number of rule tokens and the goal management needed. BETTERAVEN differs mainly in holding more goals in memory and solves nearly all items; FAIRAVEN solves about the first half.
numbers: Known only through citing papers read this session (Unsworth and Engle 2005; Little et al. 2014).
limits: Original paper not opened; description taken from the two papers that test it.
agent_relevance: Source of the idea that difficulty equals number of rules held. Dokic et al. 2025 and others show this alone does not predict who fails; measure difficulty empirically.

source: Unsworth and Engle (2005) Working memory capacity and fluid abilities: examining the correlation between Operation Span and Raven, Intelligence 33, 67-81
finding: Test of the capacity account on Raven APM Set II. The Ospan-Raven correlation did not rise with item difficulty (item 1 r=.26, item 24 r=.26).
numbers: N=160 (age 18-35, Georgia Tech and community). Ospan mean 13.25 (SD 6.58); Raven mean 18.93 (SD 7.30); r=.335. A larger lab sample gave r(1042)=.349.
quote: the relation between Operation Span and Raven is fairly constant across levels of difficulty, memory load, and rule type
limits: Single WM measure (Ospan) and low overall r=.34, which Little et al. 2014 show can hide a rise. Only 47% finished the test; 80% attempted the first 27 items.
agent_relevance: Origin of the attention control, not capacity, reading. For our agent: do not read a flat link as proof that load is irrelevant.

source: Unsworth and Engle (2005), quartile analysis
finding: Splitting items into accuracy quartiles gave a flat Ospan link in quartiles 1-3 and none in the hardest quartile.
numbers: Quartile accuracy .83, .69, .44, .18. Correlations with Ospan: Q1 .324, Q2 .294, Q3 .331, Q4 .079 (ns).
limits: The hard quartile is confounded with non-attempt and floor: only 47% of people reached the end. Authors say only quartiles 1-3 should be interpreted.
agent_relevance: A flat curve plus floor is not evidence of no load effect. Check floor before concluding.

source: Unsworth and Engle (2005), memory-load test using FAIRAVEN/BETTERAVEN item classes and rule tokens
finding: Items solvable by both Carpenter models correlated more with Ospan than items only BETTERAVEN could solve, the reverse of the capacity prediction. More rule tokens gave a weaker link.
numbers: r(both)=.36 vs r(BETTERAVEN only)=.16 in the full sample; among the 76 who finished, .31 vs .16. Rule-token accuracy and r with Ospan: 1 token .72 (r=.342), 2 tokens .66 (.276), 3 tokens .32 (.245), 4 tokens .25 (.113, ns).
limits: Hard items have low accuracy and less variance, which lowers correlation mechanically (Smolen and Chuderski 2015). High-WM people finished the test less often (25% vs 71% for low WM), a selection issue.
agent_relevance: More rules gave a lower link to WM, not a higher one. Rule count and difficulty are different things.

source: Wiley, Jarosz, Cushen and Colflesh (2011) New rule use drives the relation between working memory capacity and Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices, JEP:LMC 37, 256-263
finding: OSPAN correlated with each of 36 Raven APM items, and the correlation did not increase with item position. Items needing a new rule combination showed the highest WM link. Rule-token count did not raise the link.
numbers: Overall OSPAN-RAPM r about .33 (simulation in Little et al. used 255 synthetic subjects to mirror it). Link by rule tokens 1,2,3,4: r=.25,.24,.33,.21.
limits: Numbers taken from Little et al. 2014; original not opened. Novelty effect failed to replicate (Harrison et al. 2015; Engle lab note, N=99).
agent_relevance: Suggests novelty of a rule, not count, drives load. For an agent: first-time rule combinations may matter more than long rule lists.

source: Salthouse (1993) Raven item analysis (as cited by Unsworth and Engle 2005 and Little et al. 2014)
finding: Early null result: Raven-WM correlations did not rise with item difficulty even with a high overall r=.59 (OSPAN and sentence span).
numbers: Overall r=.59; four age groups (about 20, 20-39, 40-59, 60-79).
limits: Little et al. 2014 argue the high r is inflated by pooling age groups (WMC-age r=-.54), so the within-group r was lower. Not opened; DOI is from memory and unverified.
agent_relevance: A pooled, age-mixed sample can fake a strong link. Keep populations homogeneous when comparing our models.

source: Little, Lewandowsky and Craig (2014) Working memory capacity and fluid abilities: the more difficult the item, the more more is better, Front Psychol 5:239
finding: Reanalysis argues the flat item-wise curve is a statistical artifact of a low overall correlation. With four WM tasks pooled, the item-wise link rises with difficulty.
numbers: Study 1 N=126 after exclusions (130 tested), RAPM Set II, 4 WM tasks (memory updating, OSPAN, sentence span, spatial STM). Composite zWMC-RAPM r=.56. Item-wise slope .004-.005, t(34)=2.87, p<.01, r2=.20. OSPAN alone r=.36, slope ns (t(34)=1.39, p>.05, r2=.05).
quote: invariance can only be observed if the overall correlation between Raven's and WMC is low
limits: Items 1-3 near ceiling so their r is near 0, which drives the slope. A second study with RSPM (supplement, not read) replicated a reduced effect. Point-biserial across items is itself problematic.
agent_relevance: Weak measurement hides capacity effects. Use several probes, not one, when estimating load dependence in a model.

source: Little et al. (2014), simulation
finding: Simulation with Wiley et al. parameters shows the item-wise correlation slope grows as the overall correlation grows. At rho=.30 the curve is flat, as observed.
numbers: Bivariate normal, OSPAN M=.61 SD=.15, RAPM M=.55 SD=.16, 255 synthetic subjects, 10,000 replications, rho set to .10,.30,.50,.70,.80,.90.
limits: Model builds binary item accuracy from total scores; the slope follows from ceiling on early items.
agent_relevance: A cheap check for any agent benchmark: simulate the null before reading a flat difficulty curve as meaningful.

source: Little et al. (2014), bootstrap and rule-token analysis
finding: Bootstrapping the observed 126x36 matrix to lower r reproduces the flat curve at r about .23. Multilevel logistic regression found a WMC x rule-token interaction.
numbers: Bootstrap overall r=.53, .23, .09, slope shrinks with r. Rule tokens (Box-Tidwell exponent 2.32): token beta=-0.10 (SE .005); zWMC beta=0.54 (.12); zWMC x tokens beta=0.02 (.007), p<.01. Position exponent 1.704. With OSPAN only, the position interaction p=.09. Novelty effect not found.
limits: Rule-token coding covers a subset of items (Carpenter excluded some). Interaction is small (0.02 logit units per token).
agent_relevance: Support for the capacity view in a high-r sample; the rule-token effect is small compared with the main effects.

source: Smolen and Chuderski (2015) The quadratic relationship between difficulty of intelligence test items and their correlations with working memory, Front Psychol 6:1270
finding: Analytic and simulation proof that load-dependent correlation is mainly a function of ceiling and floor. Early ceiling with late non-floor items gives a rise; late floor gives a fall; Raven gives an inverted U.
numbers: Moderate overall r is relatively immune to ceiling/floor, so only minor changes are expected for many tests.
quote: no changes in correlation due to varying WM/Gf load, or lack of them, can yield an argument for or against any theory of WM/Gf
limits: Mathematical argument; empirical part uses Raven only.
agent_relevance: Key warning: item-wise correlation tests are uninformative. Use IRT or a direct manipulation of load instead.

source: Smolen and Chuderski (2015), empirical test
finding: In a large sample the item-wise Raven-WM link was an inverted U in item difficulty, not linear.
numbers: N=347, three complex span tasks (mean z). Item accuracy from .92 down to .09 (chance .125). Linear slope .02 [-.05,.10], F(1,34)=0.4, p=.53. Segmented fit: breakpoint error rate .44 [.14,.61], slope before .23, after -.46, adj R2=.17, F(2)=4.73, p=.02. r=.46 (n=21 easier items), r=-.52 (n=15 harder items). Quadratic term -0.43 [-0.76,-0.10].
limits: One sample, unreplicated; item error rate estimated in the same sample.
agent_relevance: A flat linear fit hid a real curved pattern. Fit non-linear shapes when plotting model accuracy against load.

source: Harrison, Shipstead and Engle (2015) Why is working memory capacity related to matrix reasoning tasks? Mem Cogn 43, 389-396
finding: Conceptual replication of Wiley et al. with an experimental novelty manipulation. Novel-rule-combination problems related less to WMC than repeated-rule problems, the opposite of Wiley.
numbers: About 208 participants (n=103 and n=105 in two counterbalanced orders). WMC composite (OSpan, SymSpan, RunSpan): novel total r=.36 vs repeated total r=.50, z(205)=-2.29, p=.02. Within orders: repeated .57 and .45, novel .47 and .27. Relation to letter sets and number series unchanged.
limits: Problems paired by rule combination; supports a learning-efficiency account (WM keeps how earlier problems were solved).
agent_relevance: WM helps carry over a solution method from the previous item. For our agent: reuse of a solved pattern is a memory benefit, not a pure load effect.

source: Salthouse and Pink (2008) Why is working memory related to fluid intelligence? Psychon Bull Rev 15, 364-371
finding: The Gf-WM link was as strong at the smallest set sizes and first trials as at larger set sizes. The authors conclude it does not depend on the amount held.
numbers: Nearly 1,000 adults. Latent Gf-WM correlation .86 (.78 age-partialled) in Study 1; .74 (.66) in Study 2. Gf with span at each set size r=.47-.53 (OSpan, study 1), .57-.61 (SSpan, study 1); Gf coefficient slightly greater at higher set sizes.
quote: the relation between working memory and fluid intelligence is not dependent on the amount of information that must be maintained
limits: Tests the load idea from the WM side (vary span set size), not the Gf side. Heavy adult-age mix.
agent_relevance: Mirror-image test: even at trivial memory loads a WM task correlates with reasoning, so capacity per se may not be the shared factor.

source: Embretson (1995) The role of working memory capacity and general control processes in intelligence, Intelligence 20, 169-189
finding: Cited as an early model-based test of WM capacity versus general control processes in abstract reasoning.
numbers: No numbers recorded; not opened.
limits: Not opened. Seen only in the Smolen and Chuderski 2015 reference list.
agent_relevance: Possible model-based item difficulty approach; read before building our difficulty measure.

source: Dokic, Koso-Drljevic and Bilalic (2025) Past reflections, present insights: a systematic review and new empirical research into the WMC-Gf relationship, Intelligence 108, 101874
finding: Systematic review finds conceptual inconsistencies, varied analyses and mixed evidence. A few studies (e.g. Little et al. 2014) support the capacity account, most do not.
numbers: Review study count not shown on the abstract page.
limits: Only the repository abstract page was opened. Full text is paywalled (Elsevier 403; Unpaywall says closed).
agent_relevance: Overall verdict: the capacity prediction is not reliably borne out. Plan with that uncertainty.

source: Dokic et al. (2025), new empirical study
finding: Capacity hypothesis not supported when task demand is item difficulty or rule tokens per item. SEM and latent growth curve models also fail to support it.
numbers: N=543, non-Anglo-Saxon sample. WMC: Operation Span, Reading Span, Symmetry Span. Gf: Raven APM items.
limits: Abstract only. No coefficients, fit indices or slopes seen. Rule-token coding source not stated.
agent_relevance: Corrects first draft: rule count alone is not a valid difficulty measure. Measure difficulty from observed results.

source: Kyllonen and Christal (1990) Reasoning ability is (little more than) working-memory capacity?!, Intelligence 14, 389-433
finding: Founding correlational claim of a very high latent link between reasoning and WM.
numbers: Commonly cited latent correlations .80 to .88 (from memory, not opened).
limits: Not opened. Later work (Ackerman et al. 2005; Kane et al. 2005) puts the link lower, around .5 to .6 shared variance.
agent_relevance: Explains why capacity is a candidate cause, but the link to difficulty is a separate test.

source: Ackerman, Beier and Boyle (2005) meta-analysis and Kane et al. (2005), as reported in Little et al. 2014
finding: Range of WM-Raven correlations in the meta-analysis is wide, which sets the expected overall r.
numbers: Ackerman et al. 2005 range .312 to .641; Kane et al. 2005 about 50% shared variance WMC-Gf.
limits: Secondary report read this session; meta-analysis itself not opened.
agent_relevance: A range this wide explains why single studies disagree on whether load matters.

source: Smolen and Chuderski (2015), literature framing of competing accounts
finding: Rejected capacity on null item-wise results: Salthouse 1993 and 2014, Unsworth and Engle 2005, Salthouse and Pink 2008, Wiley et al. 2011, favouring attention control. Capacity defenders: Cowan 2006, Colom 2008, Chuderski 2012. Relational integration (Oberauer 2008) is a third account.
numbers: WMC can explain between half (Kane 2005) and all of Gf variance (Oberauer 2008; Chuderski 2013).
limits: Review prose only.
agent_relevance: Competing accounts: capacity, attention control, relational integration. Our scaffold should test binding load, not only item count.

source: Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) beat humans on a novel text matrix task built to match Raven SPM rule structure. Difficulty depended on rule type and number of unique rules, not just total rules.
numbers: Digit Matrices: humans N=40; SPM comparison N=80. GPT-3 vs human OR=1.88 (p=.005) generative, OR=6.27 (p=2.3e-8) multiple choice. Problem type OR=.5 (generative). Unique rules, total rules held constant: human OR=.61 (p=.0047), GPT-3 OR=.25 (p=3e-10). Progression vs none: human OR=.41, GPT-3 OR=.07. Subtype pattern human vs GPT-3 r(30)=.39.
limits: GPT-3 with no prompt; text-only digits, so no perception load. GPT-4 only preliminary.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test: unique relations and progression rules drive difficulty more than raw rule count, and the LLM degrades faster than humans with unique rules.

source: Haznitrama, Ardi and Oh (2026) A neuropsychologically grounded evaluation of LLM cognitive abilities (NeuroCognition), arXiv 2603.02540
finding: Benchmark with Raven-style matrices (RAPM), spatial WM and Wisconsin Card Sorting for 10 LLMs vs 11 humans. Difficulty lowers LLM scores (p<.001). Models do better on text than image, humans the opposite.
numbers: Human RAPM: 0.430/0.444 text MC/Gen vs 0.814 image. RAPM Text MC vs Gen: GPT-5 .540 vs .605, Claude .560 vs .385, Grok 4 Fast .690 vs .555. Disabling reasoning helped Text MC (p=.021). SWM: humans .963 (image easy), .878 (hard); several LLMs near 0 on image hard even with full history; GPT-5 .631 to .989 when text added. Factor analysis of 156 models.
limits: Human sample N=11. Maintenance demand removed for LLMs by giving full history, so only manipulation load is tested.
agent_relevance: Humans fail by remembering, LLMs by manipulating even when given the state. Human capacity tests do not carry over; test manipulation load directly. Long reasoning hurt on multiple choice.

source: Li (2025) A study of rule omission in Raven's Progressive Matrices, arXiv 2510.03127
finding: Seq-to-seq transformers trained from scratch on I-RAVEN lose accuracy on omitted rules, and more when two rules are omitted than one.
numbers: Mean accuracy 47.00% (1 rule removed) to 31.47% (2 removed), different-rule condition; same-rule 92.62% to 93.42%. Remove-1 token accuracy 66.32% (3x3) to 96.88% (Center). Vision models under 30% on two-rule removal.
limits: Small models trained from scratch, not prompted LLMs. Short paper, minimal analysis. Tests generalisation, not capacity.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Unfamiliar rules hurt more than familiar ones, loosely like the Wiley novelty idea.

source: Camposampiero, Hersche, Wattenhofer, Sebastian and Rahimi (2025) I-RAVEN-X, arXiv 2510.17496
finding: Symbolic Raven benchmark that increases operand count and attribute range. LLMs collapse on arithmetic rules at larger load; reasoning models degrade much less.
numbers: Arithmetic accuracy: reasoning models 80.5% to 63.0%; LLMs 59.3% to 4.4%. Under perceptual uncertainty reasoning models lose 61.8% task accuracy.
limits: Load here is operands and value range, not rule count. Per-model numbers are in the paper table, not recorded.
agent_relevance: Load clearly matters for LLMs when it scales operands and digits, unlike the flat human item-wise curve. Use operand count as a measured difficulty axis.

source: Gong, Wan and Wang (2024) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study, AAAI 38; arXiv 2305.03731
finding: gpt-3.5-turbo on verbal and spatial n-back: performance falls significantly as n rises, a capacity limit like humans. Chain-of-thought prompting improved spatial n-back. Larger grids helped.
numbers: Declines with n in hit rate and d-prime; exact values are in figures, not recorded.
limits: Single older model; no Raven test; read abstract and discussion paragraphs only.
agent_relevance: A load-dependent limit exists in LLMs for sequential tracking. Related to hold-many-things, not to rule induction.

source: Backward digit span and fluid reasoning in 15 frontier LLMs (escholarship qt28m3k4g4)
finding: Near-perfect forward digit span but sharp failure on backward span; backward span correlated with text-based Raven's and ARC-AGI-1.
numbers: From a search snippet only: 15 models. No coefficients obtained.
limits: PDF download failed; snippet only. Title and authors unknown. Verify before use.
agent_relevance: Possible LLM version of the WM-Gf link: manipulation span, not storage, may predict reasoning.

source: Carpenter et al. (1990) rule taxonomy and token coding, as summarised in Little et al. 2014
finding: Lower-WM people were hypothesised to manage fewer rule tokens. Rule taxonomy: constant, pairwise progression, figure addition/subtraction, distribution of 3, distribution of 2.
numbers: Tokens coded 1 to 4 per item; some items excluded for technical reasons.
limits: Coding is by hand, not a validated difficulty measure. Two tests (Unsworth and Engle; Wiley) found no rise in WM link with tokens.
agent_relevance: Warning that rule-token count is coded by hand; replace it with measured difficulty.

source: Salthouse (2000) reanalysis of Salthouse (1993), as reported in Little et al. 2014
finding: Unique variance remained in the age-hardest-Raven relation after controlling for easy items, consistent with a rising link with difficulty.
numbers: No numbers in the secondary source.
limits: Secondary report only; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Hard items carry information beyond easy items. Keep hard items in any evaluation set.
